items.title: A coin doesn't 'owe' you a head after 10 tails — but a casino does
items.claim: 10 tails in a row. Probability of the next flip being heads is still 1/2. The coin has no memory. Casinos exploit the gambler's fallacy — players betting against 'streaks' actually have no edge.
items.prompt: Why doesn't the law of large numbers help short-term?

options.text: The law of large numbers only applies to dice

LLN guarantees long-run frequency convergence to expected probability, but does NOT mean short-term deviations must be 'corrected' by reverse outcomes. Each flip is independent: past results carry no information
Tails must come back to balance heads

items.reveal_title: Gambler's fallacy and the law of large numbers (correctly stated)
items.reveal:
Gambler's fallacy: the false belief that, in a sequence of independent random events, recent 'streaks' make the opposite outcome more likely.

Monte Carlo Casino, 1913: black came up 26 times in a row at a roulette table. Players reportedly lost millions betting on red, believing the streak 'must' end. Each spin was independent; the probability of red on the 27th spin was the same as on the first (~18/37 for a European wheel, less than 1/2 because of the green zero).

LLN says: as n increases, the SAMPLE PROPORTION approaches the TRUE PROBABILITY. After 10 tails in a row out of 10 flips, the proportion is 100% tails. After a million more fair flips (with roughly 500,000 each side), the cumulative proportion approaches 50%. But this happens by SWAMPING the early streak, not by REVERSING it. The next flip after 10 tails is still 50/50.

Inverse mistake (hot-hand fallacy): assuming streaks WILL continue (sports). Actually mixed evidence — some sports skills appear to genuinely streak (basketball shooting under some studies), others don't. Distinguishing real streaks from spurious ones requires careful statistics.

Gambler's fallacy explains casino profits even when individual games are 'fair-ish'. House edges (~5% in roulette) compound over many bets; players betting against streaks don't gain anything.

The broader cognitive pattern: humans expect randomness to be uniform. Real randomness has clusters and streaks. Mistaking real randomness for 'patterns' is one of the most consistently studied errors in cognitive psychology.
items.why: Past results feel like they should influence future probabilities. They don't, for independent events. Misunderstanding this drives gambling losses, conspiracy theories, and bad predictions across domains.

items.title: The most important open problem in mathematics
items.claim: Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all non-trivial zeros of the zeta function lie on the line Re(s) = 1/2. The conjecture controls the distribution of primes among integers. Proving (or disproving) it has been unsolved for 165 years.
items.prompt: Why do we care about complex zeros of a strange function?

options.text: The distribution of prime numbers is encoded in the zeros of the Riemann zeta function — proving the Riemann hypothesis would establish a vast number of theorems in number theory that are currently conditional on it
It tells us the value of zeta at integer points
It's part of the definition of pi

items.reveal:
Riemann's only paper on number theory (1859) defined the analytic continuation of the zeta function and noted that the function has 'trivial zeros' at -2, -4, -6, ... and other 'non-trivial zeros' in the strip 0 less than Re(s) less than 1. He conjectured all non-trivial zeros lie exactly on Re(s) = 1/2.

The Prime Number Theorem (Hadamard, de la Vallée Poussin, 1896) says the count of primes up to x is asymptotically x / ln x. The Riemann hypothesis would tighten the error term enormously.

Thousands of theorems in modern number theory are stated 'assuming RH'. A proof would make them unconditional. Conversely, a disproof would force major rewrites.

The first 10 trillion non-trivial zeros have all been computed and verified to lie on Re(s) = 1/2 (Gourdon, 2004). This doesn't prove the hypothesis.

The Clay Mathematics Institute lists it as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, with a $1,000,000 reward. So far, only Poincaré (Perelman, 2003) has been solved.
items.why: Primes look like a chaotic distribution. The Riemann hypothesis says they have hidden, beautiful regularity controlled by complex analysis — and 165 years of effort haven't proved or disproved it.

items.title: A 95% confidence interval does NOT mean there's a 95% chance the true value is in it
items.claim: Common claim: 'we are 95% confident the mean is between 4.2 and 5.7'. Often interpreted as 'there's a 95% probability the true mean is in this range'. In frequentist statistics this interpretation is technically wrong.
items.prompt: What does a 95% confidence interval actually mean?

options.text: The probability the parameter is in the interval is 95%

If you repeated the experiment many times and constructed a CI each time, 95% of those intervals would contain the true value. For a single interval, the true value is either in it or not — the 95% refers to the procedure's long-run reliability, not to a probability about the parameter
It's the same as a Bayesian credible interval

items.reveal:
In FREQUENTIST statistics, the true parameter (e.g., true mean mu) is treated as fixed, not random. The interval is random because it depends on the random sample. The interval either contains mu or it doesn't — probability 0 or 1.

The '95%' is a property of the PROCEDURE for generating the interval: across many hypothetical replications of the experiment, 95% of the intervals would contain the true mu. For your one observed interval, it either contains mu or doesn't.

In BAYESIAN statistics, the parameter is treated as random (described by a posterior distribution). A 95% credible interval IS the range where the parameter has 95% posterior probability of lying. The Bayesian interpretation is the one most people intuitively want.

Frequentist CIs and Bayesian credible intervals often look similar numerically — but they mean different things. The interpretation matters for inference and communication.

Why this distinction matters:
- Misinterpreting CIs leads to overconfidence in single results.
- Policy debates often hang on whether 'we are 95% sure' means anything actionable.
- Multiple comparisons (running many tests, picking 'significant' ones) inflate apparent CI coverage — see also: replication crisis.

Many statisticians (including Hoekstra et al. 2014) have shown that researchers across disciplines misinterpret CIs.

For most practical purposes, the Bayesian interpretation 'works'. But understanding the frequentist meaning matters for understanding what randomized inference does and doesn't guarantee.
items.why: Statistical results are commonly miscommunicated. Confidence intervals are a famous example: most users (including professionals) believe an interpretation the statistics don't support. Understanding the distinction is part of statistical literacy.
